assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged pattern at line 479 is a human-readable date parser used by parseSceneDateParts to extract scene dates from roleplay message content. The static unsafe-regex signal is a ReDoS heuristic rather than a demonstrated vulnerability: the pattern's alternations (weekday and month names, ordinal suffixes) are distinctive literal alternatives without nested quantified ambiguity that would produce exponential backtracking. Input is local chat text processed in the browser with an abort guard around detection; no network destination, credential handling, or persistence of attacker-controlled data is involved in the supplied evidence. In the worst theoretical case a crafted message could cause a transient UI delay, which is a recoverable local performance effect and does not rise to material harm. No concrete attacker-controlled path to data loss, exfiltration, or code execution is demonstrated.
assessments.layman_explanation: This is just a pattern for recognizing a date, like a weekday and month spelling, inside story messages so the extension can figure out when the story is happening. It runs entirely on your own computer and does not send data anywhere or change files. A strange message could at most briefly pause the page.
assessments.developer_action: No change required. Optional hardening: cap the length of message lines before applying the date pattern.

assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged pattern at line 1983 extracts a Wandlight preset version token from the notes field of a SillyTavern preset. It is a short, linear pattern with a single bounded digit group and no nested quantifiers, so the unsafe-regex heuristic does not correspond to demonstrated catastrophic backtracking. The input is the notes text of the user's own locally stored presets, and the result is used only to compare preset versions and drive UI status messages. The surrounding code shows preset installation is user-confirmed and version parsing feeds local comparison logic only. No credential exposure, network destination, or attacker-controlled execution path is present in the supplied evidence.
assessments.layman_explanation: This pattern reads a version number out of a preset description so the extension can tell whether the bundled preset is newer. It only looks at text on your own machine, does not send anything anywhere, and does not take any action by itself.

assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged line creates SVG elements using the standard SVG namespace identifier. The scanned signal is categorized as a shady link because a URL-like literal appears in a createElementNS call, but the literal is the fixed W3C SVG namespace used by every SVG creation helper in this UI code. There is no external request, no user-controlled destination, and no data flow leaving the extension. The surrounding functions construct in-memory DOM for a lore timeline visualization and never transmit the namespace value.
assessments.layman_explanation: This flag is just the standard SVG namespace used to draw charts in the lore timeline. It is a harmless technical identifier, not a link to any website, and nothing is sent anywhere.

assessments.technical_explanation: The flagged command executes a fixed git command to enumerate repository files for a local secret-scanning script. The command string is constant; no attacker-controlled input is interpolated into it, and it is run with standard error and output piping. The script is developer tooling, not shipped extension runtime code. Its purpose is defensive: scanning tracked and untracked text files for API keys and private key material and failing the run on findings. No exfiltration or unexpected code execution is present.
assessments.layman_explanation: This is a developer helper that lists project files with git so it can check them for accidentally committed secrets. It only runs a fixed harmless command and does not send data anywhere.

assessments.technical_explanation: The scanner flagged a version-parsing regular expression used on provider preset version strings. The pattern matches a bounded digit-and-dot version sequence with no nested quantifiers or ambiguous backtracking states, so it is not a ReDoS risk under realistic input lengths. The data being matched comes from local preset metadata and is used only to compare version numbers. No untrusted network input, no evaluation of matched content, and no security boundary is crossed. Similar version-matching logic appears nearby for the same benign purpose.
assessments.layman_explanation: This flag is a version-number matching pattern used to tell if a preset is outdated. It is simple and safe, and it only reads local preset labels to compare versions.

limitations: This advisory review cannot prove the absence of unknown behavior.
